ch08.mcq.text:
<!-- Answer key, Chapter 8 (for instructors; HTML comments are removed from every rendered format):
     1 C, 2 A, 3 D, 4 B, 5 D, 6 B, 7 C, 8 A, 9 D, 10 C, 11 B, 12 A, 13 C, 14 D, 15 A.
     1 C: a test on an incomplete extract cannot find problems in records that were never extracted.
     2 A: large items are examined individually, and the strata that hold most of the value get the most careful tests.
     3 D: Benford's Law expects LOG10(2), about 30 percent, of amounts to begin with 1.
     4 B: scientific notation always starts with the first significant digit, including amounts below $1.
     5 D: a MAD of 0.013 is marginally acceptable; with so many amounts, chi-square flags even small differences.
     6 B: partial payments come only from invoices of $1,000 or more, a subset selected by size.
     7 C: check numbers are assigned, not measured, so they carry no information about magnitude.
     8 A: the payment came after the as-of date, and the invoice was 46 days past due on December 31.
     9 D: an unexplained difference means the ledger holds unsupported amounts or the detail is incomplete.
     10 C: the standard requires the estimate to reflect remote risks and accepts aging-based methods.
     11 B: entries posted automatically for each sales invoice are routine, not a characteristic of fraudulent entries.
     12 A: INT removes the time, so the flag is TRUE when the entry was created after the date it posts to.
     13 C: a risk score ranks entries for review; it is not a probability of fraud.
     14 D: RANDARRAY recalculates, so only pasted values preserve the selection as evidence.
     15 A: check numbers follow the numbering of all payments, so ACH and wire payments leave gaps. -->

ch09.mcq.text:
<!-- Answer key, Chapter 9 (for instructors; HTML comments are removed from every rendered format):
     1 B, 2 D, 3 A, 4 C, 5 C, 6 A, 7 D, 8 B, 9 A, 10 D, 11 B, 12 C, 13 A, 14 D, 15 B.
     1 B: a column list separated by commas returns just those columns.
     2 D: GLEntry.AccountID is the Account table's surrogate key; 5080 has AccountID 93.
     3 A: = compares text exactly, including case; the stored value is WorkOrderClose.
     4 C: dates stored as year-month-day text are compared with dates written the same way, in quotes.
     5 C: AND is evaluated before OR, so the condition adds every 2026 posting of every account.
     6 A: no comparison with NULL is true; IS NULL finds the missing values.
     7 D: DISTINCT reveals the values in use, so a filter is not written for a value that does not exist.
     8 B: DESC sorts from the largest, and LIMIT 10 keeps the first ten rows.
     9 A: without ORDER BY, LIMIT returns an undefined selection of rows.
     10 D: a working copy keeps the download safe; DB Browser opens files for writing unless opened read-only, and a SELECT never changes a file.
     11 B: without the comma, AccountName becomes an alias for AccountNumber, a logical error.
     12 C: the clauses must be written as SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
     13 A: % matches any run of characters; = compares the pattern literally, _ matches exactly one character, and IN needs an exact value.
     14 D: documentation lets another person understand, rerun, and review the queries.
     15 B: two whole numbers divide as whole numbers, a decimal keeps the fraction, and text never equals a number when
     neither side is a column; SELECT needs no FROM. -->
